There was a lot of talk last year about fighting involution and reversing excess capacity, but while capacity has indeed declined, according to Caixin it hasn't declined by nearly enough to end severe overcapacity problems in the solar industry.

"China’s newly installed solar capacity plummeted 66% year-on-year in the first half of 2026 as the sector grappled with overcapacity and depressed prices. Since the start of 2026, the prices of polysilicon, wafers and solar cells have dropped 42.3%, 28.7% and 27.7%, respectively. The module price was an exception, edging up 3%. Under the current circumstances, major solar manufacturers are struggling to turn a profit."

In some ways this is good for the world, as China's huge losses and transfers effectively subsidize global new solar installations, but, like Japan in the 1980s, China may be bankrupting itself to keep excess capacity from reversing. This is certainly what its debt numbers suggest.
https://t.co/p3O7QXglgA

Caixin: "Local governments are struggling to stockpile high-quality projects, which inherently limits their capacity for countercyclical fiscal expansion."

In the past any time economic activity dropped to below a politically-determined minimum level, local governments responded "countercyclically" with large increases in spending, especially on infrastructure, whether or not these generated positive economic returns. In China, economic problems are almost always described as cyclical rather than structural, which is why the rection to any slowdown has usually been to double down on the existing growth model.

But as the costs to this strategy have accumulated – in the form of the second highest debt-to-GDP ratio in the world (after Japan's) and the fastest-growing debt-to-GDP ratio in history – it has become increasingly hard for local governments to continue this strategy.

However rather than abandon the strategy of using increasingly non-productive investment to meet political growth targets, i.e. rather than acknowledge the structural nature of the problem, it seems that Beijing will instead just shift the borrowing onto the central government balance sheets.

I think this is likely to be a mistake for the Chinese economy over the longer term, but I also think it is politically hard for them not to make this mistake.

I don't really agree. These global imbalances have been a problem for decades for American workers and the US manufacturing sector, and you can see that very clearly from the 1980s in rising debt and in the way median income growth stagnated even as productivity continued to grow, which in turn has created terrible levels of income inequality.

Of course not all sectors suffered. The associated financial inflows, the ease of relocating production facilities abroad, and the disinflationary impacts strongly benefitted bankers, creditors, and owners of movable capital, and as long as they had the political upper hand, Washington did not treat the trade imbalances as a problem even though there had been urgent complaints from many parts of the economy, not least in the 1990s and 2010s. 

This is actually an old story in US history. Whenever income inequality and the associated political capture has reached high enough levels (e.g. 1830s, 1890s, 1920s) there has eventually been a "Jacksonian" revolt that forced a shift in domestic politics. 

I would say that this shift in domestic politics mattered more than the rise of China today and Japan in the 1980s as serious geopolitical rivals. It was only because their economies became so big that their imbalances began to matter so much mote to their trade partners.

Some problems with your proposed "remedies" here. First, what would be the basis for prohobiting US cloud providers from hosting Chinese open weight models? No US providers are faciliting access to Chinese model APIs. Many companies, including startups, have already built production applications on top of Chinese open weight models, fine tuning, adding value etc. What would be the justification for not allowing this, have not heard any credible argument here. Second, what is the justification for not allowing remote access by Chinese model developers to overseas data centers to train models? This has not happened and is clearly too difficult to enforce if there was a decision to try and again over extend US export controls to overseas cloud providers. It is too late to do this in any case.  All of this appears to just be an extension of Gina Raimondo's Fool's Errand here, that like the October 2022 export controls, will end up damaging US companies and the US economy more than it will produce any gains for national security....
